title: Not many words (Matthew 6:7–8)
hook: your Father knows what you need before you ask

segments.voice: Yesterday, not to be seen, and your line was the father sees in secret. Did you do one good thing and tell no one? Day two hundred forty-nine.

Some people feel they can't pray because they don't know the right words. They've heard others pray beautifully, long flowing sentences, and they freeze. Others pray the way we write emails to someone important: carefully, at length, explaining everything, just in case. Both are really asking the same question: how much do I have to say to be heard? Right after telling his listeners to shut the door and pray in secret, Jesus answers that question.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW THE RIGHT WORDS.` → `PRAYING LIKE A LONG EMAIL.` → `HOW MUCH DO I HAVE TO SAY?`

segments.voice: When you pray, he says, don't babble on, thinking you'll be heard because of your many words. The Greek verb here is battalogeo. It appears nowhere else in the New Testament, and hardly anywhere in Greek before it. Nobody knows exactly where it comes from. Many scholars think it's a sound word, like our blah-blah-blah: batta-batta. Heaping up syllables. Then the reason, in the King James Bible: "your Father knoweth what things ye have need of, before ye ask him." Stop and feel how freeing that is. You're not informing God. You're not filing a report. He already knows. So why pray at all? Christians have asked that for two thousand years, and the usual answer is: because prayer isn't mainly for passing on information. It's for being with someone. A child who says I'm hungry isn't telling their mother something she doesn't know. They're turning toward her. Now, a fair question: what about repeating prayers? Christians read this verse in different ways. Many Catholics pray the rosary, and Orthodox Christians repeat the Jesus Prayer, and they say the warning is against empty words, not repeated ones. After all, in Gethsemane, Mark says Jesus "went away, and prayed, and spake the same words." Some Protestant Christians hear the verse as a caution against praying by rote, and favor praying in their own words. Both agree on the heart: it's not the number of words that reaches God. The very next thing Jesus does is teach a short prayer. Tomorrow, we'll look at it again.
screen: `BATTALOGEO: BLAH-BLAH-BLAH.` · `HE KNOWETH BEFORE YE ASK.` · `PRAYER: TURNING TOWARD SOMEONE.` · `EMPTY WORDS, NOT REPEATED ONES.` · then, large: `YOUR FATHER KNOWETH WHAT THINGS YE HAVE NEED OF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray in ten words or fewer. Settle, and breathe. Think of the thing that's weighing on you most today. Now shrink it down. Not a paragraph. Ten words or fewer. Help my mother. I'm afraid about tomorrow. Thank you for this morning. If you pray, say those few words to God, once, and then just sit, trusting that he already knows the rest. If you don't pray, simply name it, and let the silence hold it. The bell holds the time.
Not many words. Don't babble on to be heard; your Father knows what you need before you ask.
Your line: he already knows. Today, when a worry comes, put it in ten words or fewer, say it once, and let it go. Day two hundred forty-nine.

howItsDone: Christians pray both in set words and in their own words: Catholics and Orthodox often use repeated prayers like the rosary and the Jesus Prayer, and many Protestants favor short spontaneous prayers; all describe prayer as turning toward God rather than informing him.

what it means: God already knows what you need; prayer is turning toward him, not filing a report.
what a scholar hears: battalogeo is almost unknown before Matthew; many think it imitates babbling, like blah-blah.

notes: Matthew 6:7 (KJV 'as the heathen do') is paraphrased without the comparison to other peoples, to keep the lesson from contrasting traditions. Keeper to confirm.
battalogeo: rare, etymology uncertain, possibly onomatopoeic (or from Aramaic battal, 'idle'). Confirm.
Readings of 'vain repetitions' across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant Christians presented without ranking.
The child/mother illustration is the script's own, not a cited source.
